gancho: O truque básico para quebrar cifras, contar quais símbolos aparecem mais, foi descrito no século IX pelo sábio árabe al-Kindi. É a explicação mais antiga conhecida de qualquer método de decifração.
explicacao: Numa cifra de substituição simples, cada letra da mensagem vira sempre o mesmo símbolo. Só que as línguas não usam as letras por igual: em cada idioma, algumas aparecem muito e outras quase nunca, numa distribuição que se repete em quase qualquer trecho de texto. Essa marca sobrevive à troca. Al-Kindi, polímata árabe do século IX, ensinou como aproveitá-la num tratado sobre decifrar correspondência cifrada: pegue um texto comum da mesma língua, de mais ou menos uma folha, conte quantas vezes aparece cada letra e ordene-as. Depois classifique do mesmo jeito os símbolos da mensagem secreta e troque o mais frequente pela letra mais frequente, o segundo pela segunda, e assim por diante. É o registro mais antigo que se conhece da análise de frequência e de qualquer tipo de criptoanálise. Há quem sugira que o estudo minucioso do texto do Alcorão revelou primeiro que o árabe tem uma frequência característica de letras. O método se espalhou e, no Renascimento, sistemas parecidos eram muito usados nos Estados europeus. Para driblá-lo, os criptógrafos passaram a usar, por exemplo, vários símbolos para as letras mais comuns, o que complicou cifrar e decifrar e abriu espaço para erros.

fontes.trecho: Frequency analysis is based on the fact that, in any given stretch of written language, certain letters and combinations of letters occur with varying frequencies. Moreover, there is a characteristic distribution of letters that is roughly the same for almost all samples of that language. [...] In a simple substitution cipher, each letter of the plaintext is replaced with another, and any particular letter in the plaintext will always be transformed into the same letter in the ciphertext. [...] The first known recorded explanation of frequency analysis (indeed, of any kind of cryptanalysis) was given in the 9th century by Al-Kindi, an Arab polymath, in A Manuscript on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages. It has been suggested that a close textual study of the Qur'an first brought to light that Arabic has a characteristic letter frequency. Its use spread, and similar systems were widely used in European states by the time of the Renaissance. [...] Homophonic substitution: Use of homophones — several alternatives to the most common letters in otherwise monoalphabetic substitution ciphers. [...] A disadvantage of all these attempts to defeat frequency counting attacks is that it increases complication of both enciphering and deciphering, leading to mistakes.

One way to solve an encrypted message, if we know its language, is to find a different plaintext of the same language long enough to fill one sheet or so, and then we count the occurrences of each letter. We call the most frequently occurring letter the "first", the next most occurring letter the "second", the following most occurring letter the "third", and so on, until we account for all the different letters in the plaintext sample. Then we look at the cipher text we want to solve and we also classify its symbols. We find the most occurring symbol and change it to the form of the "first" letter of the plaintext sample

gancho: A célebre "cifra indecifrável" de Vigenère não foi criada por Vigenère, e sim por Giovan Battista Bellaso, em 1553. E Charles Babbage quebrou uma variante dela em 1854, mas não publicou o método.
explicacao: A ideia é trocar cada letra da mensagem por outra deslocada no alfabeto, mas com um deslocamento diferente a cada letra, ditado pelas letras de uma palavra-chave. Assim, a mesma letra vira símbolos diferentes ao longo do texto. Bellaso descreveu o esquema num livro de 1553, e no século XIX a invenção foi atribuída por engano a Blaise de Vigenère, que em 1586 publicara outra cifra. O historiador David Kahn lamentou que a história tenha posto no nome de Vigenère uma cifra com que ele nada teve a ver. A fama de inquebrável rendeu o apelido francês de "cifra indecifrável". Babbage quebrou uma variante já em 1854, mas não publicou; uma hipótese é que tenha guardado o segredo por assessorar em criptografia um almirante britânico durante a Guerra da Crimeia. Em 1863, Friedrich Kasiski foi o primeiro a publicar um método geral para decifrá-la. A reputação, porém, sobreviveu: Lewis Carroll a chamou de inquebrável em 1868, num texto para uma revista infantil, e a Scientific American, em 1917, disse que ela era "impossível de traduzir". Na Guerra Civil americana, os confederados a usavam com discos de latão, e a União quebrava as mensagens deles com regularidade.

fontes.trecho: is a method of encrypting alphabetic text where each letter of the plaintext is encoded with a different Caesar cipher, whose increment is determined by the corresponding letter of another text, the key. [...] First described by Giovan Battista Bellaso in 1553, the cipher is easy to understand and implement, but it resisted all attempts to break it until 1863, three centuries later. This earned it the description le chiffrage indéchiffrable (French for 'the indecipherable cipher'). [...] In 1863, Friedrich Kasiski was the first to publish a general method of deciphering Vigenère ciphers. In the 19th century, the scheme was misattributed to Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596) and so acquired its present name. [...] In 1586 Blaise de Vigenère published a type of polyalphabetic cipher called an autokey cipher [...] David Kahn, in his book The Codebreakers, lamented this misattribution, saying that history had "ignored this important contribution and instead named a regressive and elementary cipher for him [Vigenère] though he had nothing to do with it". [...] Noted author and mathematician Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (Lewis Carroll) called the Vigenère cipher unbreakable in his 1868 piece "The Alphabet Cipher" in a children's magazine. In 1917, Scientific American described the Vigenère cipher as "impossible of translation". Charles Babbage is known to have broken a variant of the cipher as early as 1854 but did not publish his work. One hypothesis is that he intentionally kept the general method secret, since he was a cryptographical adviser to his friend, Rear-Admiral Sir Francis Beaufort, during the Crimean War. [...] The Confederate States of America, for example, used a brass cipher disk to implement the Vigenère cipher during the American Civil War. The Confederacy's messages were far from secret, and the Union regularly cracked its messages.

gancho: Maria Stuart foi condenada por cartas cifradas que julgava seguras. Elas saíam escondidas num barril de cerveja, mas cada uma era aberta, decifrada e copiada pelos espiões de Elizabeth I antes de seguir viagem.
explicacao: Presa na Inglaterra, a rainha escocesa estava proibida por decreto, desde julho de 1584, de receber ou mandar qualquer correspondência. Francis Walsingham, secretário e chefe de espionagem de Elizabeth, precisava de provas que permitissem executá-la e criou um canal que só parecia clandestino: um cervejeiro local levava as mensagens numa caixa à prova d'água dentro de um barril de cerveja. O agente duplo Gilbert Gifford servia de mensageiro, e Thomas Phelippes, especialista em cifras e línguas, ficou alojado em Chartley, onde Maria estava presa. Ele decodificava cada carta e fazia uma cópia; a original era lacrada de novo e seguia para o destino. Em julho de 1586, Maria respondeu em código a Anthony Babington e aprovou o plano de assassinar Elizabeth. Phelippes, a mando de Walsingham, guardou o original e fez uma cópia com um pedido acrescentado: os nomes dos conspiradores. No julgamento, em outubro de 1586, Maria não teve direito a advogado nem pôde examinar as provas, e trechos das traduções de Phelippes foram lidos. Ela foi decapitada em 8 de fevereiro de 1587, diante de 300 testemunhas.

fontes.trecho: After the Throckmorton Plot, Queen Elizabeth had issued a decree in July 1584, which prevented all communication to and from Mary. [...] They needed evidence for which she could be executed based on their Bond of Association tenets. Thus Walsingham established a new line of communication, one which he could carefully control without incurring any suspicion from Mary. [...] Gifford and jailer Paulet had arranged for a local brewer to facilitate the movement of messages between Queen Mary and her supporters by placing them in a watertight box inside a beer barrel. Thomas Phelippes, a cipher and language expert in Walsingham's employ, was then quartered at Chartley Hall to receive the messages, decode them and send them to Walsingham. [...] Phelippes would decode and make a copy of the letter. The letter was then resealed and given back to Gifford, who would pass it on to the brewer. [...] Mary responded in code on 17 July 1586 ordering the would-be rescuers to assassinate Queen Elizabeth. [...] But this time, Phelippes, on the direction of Walsingham, kept the original and made a copy, adding a request for the names of the conspirators: [...] In October 1586, Mary was sent to be tried at Fotheringhay Castle in Northamptonshire by 46 English lords, bishops and earls. She was not permitted legal counsel, not permitted to review the evidence against her, nor to call witnesses. Portions of Phellipes' letter translations were read at the trial. [...] on 8 February 1587, in front of 300 witnesses, Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed by beheading.

Mary was misled into thinking her letters were secure, while in reality, they were deciphered and read by Walsingham. From these letters, it was clear that Mary had sanctioned the attempted assassination of Elizabeth.

gancho: Um cientista da computação, um pianista e um físico acharam numa biblioteca francesa 57 cartas cifradas, catalogadas entre papéis italianos. Decifradas, eram de Maria Stuart, e quase todas eram dadas como perdidas.
explicacao: George Lasry, Norbert Biermann e Satoshi Tomokiyo procuravam cifras históricas para decifrar, sem buscar nada de Maria Stuart. Na Biblioteca Nacional da França, acharam páginas de símbolos misturadas a papéis italianos do início do século XVI, sem pista de remetente, destinatário ou data. Primeiro passaram os cerca de 150 mil símbolos para o computador. Um algoritmo que testa chaves e vai ajustando as que pontuam melhor decifrou uns 30% do texto; o resto saiu à mão, num trabalho que o estudo compara a resolver uma enorme palavra cruzada. A cifra era homofônica: cada letra podia ser escrita de vários jeitos, e havia símbolos próprios para pessoas e palavras comuns. O texto estava em francês, com expressões como "minha liberdade" e "meu filho", e a certeza veio com o nome Walsingham, o chefe de espionagem de Elizabeth I. As cartas, quase todas para o embaixador francês Michel de Castelnau, foram escritas entre 1578 e 1584, durante o cativeiro de Maria na Inglaterra. Só sete eram conhecidas, por cópias em arquivos britânicos: na época, Walsingham obtinha cópias por meio de um informante na embaixada francesa. O estudo saiu em 2023 na revista Cryptologia, e o historiador John Guy chamou o achado de o mais importante sobre Maria Stuart em 100 anos.

fontes.titulo: Code Breakers Discover—and Decipher—Long-Lost Letters by Mary, Queen of Scots (Smithsonian Magazine)
fontes.trecho: they originally decided to examine a cache of coded notes housed at the National Library of France as part of a broader push to “locate, digitize, transcribe, decipher and analyze” historic ciphers. Those pages turned out to be 57 of Mary’s encrypted letters, the majority of which were sent to Michel de Castelnau, the French ambassador to England, between 1578 and 1584. All but seven were previously thought to be lost. Interspersed with a collection of early 16th-century Italian papers, the documents were written in mysterious symbols that offered no clues “as to their sender, recipients or date,” lead author George Lasry, a computer scientist and cryptographer based in Israel, tells Smithsonian magazine. It was only when the scholars spotted the word “Walsingham”—the last name of Elizabeth’s spymaster, Francis Walsingham—that they realized the letters’ significance. [...] “This is the most important new find on Mary, Queen of Scots, for 100 years. [...] Lasry worked with Norbert Biermann, a German pianist, and Satoshi Tomokiyo, a Japanese physicist and patents expert. First, the men transcribed the documents, rendering the 150,000 symbols readable by a computer. Then they employed a hill-climbing algorithm, in which a computer tries out different cipher keys, making small changes to high-scoring keys before attempting to decipher the text again. [...] Starting from scratch, the hill-climbing algorithm managed to decrypt about 30 percent of the original text. But the remaining 70 percent had to be deciphered by hand, using a process “somewhat analogous to solving a large crossword puzzle,” according to the study. The encryption turned out to be a homophonic cipher, in which each letter of the alphabet can be encoded in several different ways. Mary also used a number of dedicated symbols representing commonly cited words and people. [...] Early on, they realized the papers were written in French, not Italian as the library’s catalog indicated. Phrases like “ma liberté” (“my freedom”) and “mon fils” (“my son”) pointed to the writer’s identity as a mother in captivity. [...] That’s when they found duplicates of the seven letters already known to historians, all written in 1583 and 1584. The timeline makes sense: During this period, Walsingham was obtaining copies of Mary’s letters from a mole in the French Embassy. [...] Lasry et al. / Cryptologia, 2023
Mary sent letters in cipher to the French ambassador to England, Michel de Castelnau, scores of which were discovered and decrypted in 2022–2023.

gancho: O Grande Cifrário de Luís XIV desafiou decifradores por séculos. Por volta de 1893, um oficial francês achou o truque: cada número valia uma sílaba, não uma letra, e alguns números serviam só para despistar.
explicacao: A cifra foi criada por Antoine Rossignol e seu filho Bonaventure, de uma família que serviu os reis franceses como criptógrafos por gerações. Antoine ficou famoso em 1626: os franceses cercavam Réalmont, cidade dos huguenotes, e tomaram de um mensageiro uma carta cifrada. No mesmo dia ele a decifrou; ela dizia que a cidade não resistiria muito, e os franceses a devolveram decifrada, forçando a rendição. O Grande Cifrário usava 587 números que representavam sílabas. Para atrapalhar a contagem de frequências, alguns eram nulos, feitos para ser ignorados, e havia armadilhas, como um número que mandava desconsiderar o anterior. Quando a cifra caiu em desuso, muitos documentos dos arquivos franceses ficaram ilegíveis, até que o comandante Étienne Bazeries, em três anos de trabalho, percebeu a lógica das sílabas. Ele apostou que a sequência 124-22-125-46-345 queria dizer "les ennemis", os inimigos, e dali desvendou o resto. Numa das cartas, Bazeries achou a ordem de prender um general na fortaleza de Pignerol e deduziu que os números desconhecidos 330 e 309 queriam dizer "máscara" e ponto final: o general seria o Homem da Máscara de Ferro. A tese é fraca: os números aparecem uma única vez, e nenhuma variante da cifra daquela época incluía essa palavra.

fontes.trecho: The Great Cipher (French: Grand chiffre) was a nomenclator cipher developed by the Rossignols, several generations of whom served the French monarchs as cryptographers. [...] After it fell out of current use, many documents in the French archives were unreadable until it was decoded. [...] Antoine Rossignol's cryptographic skills became known in 1626, when an encrypted letter was taken from a messenger leaving the city of Réalmont, controlled by the Huguenots and surrounded by the French army. The letter stated that the Huguenots would not be able to hold on to the city for much longer, and by the end of the day, Rossignol had successfully deciphered it. The French returned the letter with the deciphered message and forced the Huguenots to surrender. He and his son, Bonaventure Rossignol, were soon appointed to prominent roles in the court. Together, the two devised a cipher so strong that it baffled cryptanalysts for centuries. Commandant Étienne Bazeries managed to break the cipher around 1893 over a period of three years by realising that each number stood for a French syllable, rather than single letters, unlike traditional ciphers. He guessed that a particular sequence of repeated numbers, 124-22-125-46-345, stood for les ennemis ("the enemies") and from that information was able to unravel the entire cipher. [...] His Majesty desires that you immediately arrest General Bulonde and cause him to be conducted to the fortress of Pignerole [...] The "330" and "309" codegroups appeared only once in the correspondence, so it is impossible to confirm what they stand for. Bazeries verified General Bulonde was disgraced and removed from command, so he reasoned 330 and 309 stood for masque and a full stop. However, none of the cipher variants used in the Iron Mask period included masque, an unlikely word to include in the cipher's small repertory. [...] The basis of the code cracked by Bazeries was a set of 587 numbers that stood for syllables. [...] To counter frequency analysis, some number sets were "nulls", meant to be ignored by the intended recipient. Others were traps, including a codegroup that meant to ignore the previous codegroup.

gancho: Em 1969, o assassino do Zodíaco mandou a jornais uma cifra de 408 símbolos. FBI e CIA tentaram, mas quem a quebrou foi um casal sem formação em criptologia. Outra cifra dele, de 340 símbolos, resistiu 51 anos.
explicacao: Em 1º de agosto de 1969, três jornais da região de São Francisco receberam cartas quase idênticas de alguém que assumia ataques na cidade de Vallejo. Cada carta trazia um pedaço diferente de uma cifra de 408 símbolos, e o autor afirmava que nela estava sua identidade. FBI e CIA tentaram decifrá-la, mas quem conseguiu, em 5 de agosto, foram Donald e Bettye Harden, um casal de Salinas, nenhum dos dois criptólogo. Bettye partiu da aposta de que a palavra "kill" (matar) apareceria no texto. A mensagem, porém, não revelava nome algum. Em novembro de 1969, chegou ao San Francisco Chronicle uma cifra de 340 caracteres. Ela ficou 51 anos sem solução, até 5 de dezembro de 2020, quando foi decifrada por três particulares: o engenheiro de software americano David Oranchak, o matemático australiano Sam Blake e o programador belga Jarl Van Eycke. O programa de Van Eycke, o AZdecrypt, testou 650 mil soluções possíveis até achar a melhor chave, e um erro do próprio autor ao montar a cifra tinha tornado tudo mais difícil. O FBI confirmou a decifração e concluiu que ela não traz pistas novas sobre quem era o Zodíaco, caso que segue entre os mais famosos sem solução dos EUA. Duas cifras curtas continuam sem resposta definitiva.

fontes.trecho: Two of the Zodiac's four cryptograms were decrypted in 1969 and 2020, and the other two remain unsolved. [...] the case one of the most famous unsolved cases in American history. [...] On August 1, 1969, the Vallejo Times, San Francisco Chronicle and San Francisco Examiner all received letters written by someone taking credit for the attacks in Vallejo. The three letters were nearly identical [...] Enclosed in all three letters was a different cryptogram. They combined to form a 408-symbol cipher (Z408). The writer claimed, "In this cipher is my idenity. [sic]" [...] The decoded message did not reveal the Zodiac's identity. Both the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) attempted to decrypt the Z408 cipher. On August 5, it was cracked by Donald and Bettye Harden, a couple in Salinas. Neither was a cryptologist. Bettye deployed a crib by correctly guessing the word "kill" would appear in the message. [...] On November 8, 1969, Zodiac mailed a card with a 340-character cryptogram (Z340) to the Chronicle [...] For 51 years, the Z340 cryptogram remained unsolved until it was deciphered by an international team of private citizens on December 5, 2020. The cryptology group included American software engineer David Oranchak, Australian mathematician Sam Blake, and Belgian programmer Jarl Van Eycke. Using a program made by Van Eycke called AZdecrypt, the team ran 650,000 possible solutions for the cipher until the program came up with the best possible encryption key. The Zodiac had apparently made a mistake when creating the cipher, which made it more difficult to solve. [...] The FBI verified the decryption and concluded the decoded message provided no further clues to Zodiac's identity.

gancho: A escultura Kryptos, na sede da CIA, tem desde 1990 uma mensagem cifrada que ninguém quebrou. Em 2025, a solução surgiu por outro caminho: dois jornalistas a acharam em papéis que o artista doou a um arquivo.
explicacao: A obra de Jim Sanborn, inaugurada em 3 de novembro de 1990 em Langley, na Virgínia, traz quatro mensagens cifradas recortadas em placas de cobre. Os sistemas foram criados com Edward Scheidt, um funcionário da CIA que se aposentava e esperava que tudo fosse resolvido em cinco a dez anos. As três primeiras partes caíram: uma equipe da NSA chegou lá entre 1992 e 1993, sem divulgar, e um analista da CIA as resolveu com lápis e papel em 1998. A quarta, a K4, resistiu, e Sanborn foi soltando dicas, como as palavras BERLIN e CLOCK em posições conhecidas do texto. Em setembro de 2025, os jornalistas Jarett Kobek e Richard Byrne encontraram, entre papéis que Sanborn doara aos Archives of American Art, do Smithsonian, fragmentos que, juntos, pareciam formar o texto completo da K4. Sanborn confirmou e explicou que os incluíra por engano ao organizar documentos durante um tratamento contra o câncer. A pedido dele, o Smithsonian lacrou os papéis até 2075. Em novembro de 2025, o arquivo com a solução foi leiloado por US$ 962.500. Em junho de 2026, o comprador, uma empresa de capital de risco, lançou um desafio público para quem resolver a K4, que ainda não foi quebrada por criptoanálise.

fontes.trecho: Kryptos is a sculpture by the American artist Jim Sanborn located on the grounds of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) headquarters, the George Bush Center for Intelligence in Langley, Virginia. Since its dedication on November 3, 1990, there has been much speculation about the meaning of the four encrypted messages [...] Of these four messages, the first three have been solved, while the fourth message remains one of the most famous unsolved codes in the world. [...] are cut out of the copper plates. [...] Sanborn worked with a retiring CIA employee named Edward Scheidt to come up with the cryptographic systems used on the sculpture. [...] He said that his intention was for it to be solved in five to ten years. [...] After Gillogly's announcement, the CIA revealed that their analyst David Stein had solved the same passages in 1998 using pencil and paper techniques [...] had solved passages 1–3 in late 1992. [...] The documents show that by June 1993, a small group of NSA cryptanalysts had succeeded in solving the first three passages of the sculpture. [...] In November 2010, Sanborn released a clue, publicly stating that "NYPVTT", the 64th to 69th letters in passage 4, become "BERLIN" after decryption. Sanborn gave The New York Times another clue in November 2014: the letters "MZFPK", the 70th through 74th letters in passage 4, become "CLOCK" after decryption. [...] The Kryptos archive ultimately sold for $962,500 at the conclusion of the auction. In June 2026, the venture capital firm Paradigm disclosed that it had been the anonymous winning bidder for the archive, which included the unpublished solution to K4. The firm also launched a Kryptos website and a ten-puzzle "capture-the-flag"-style challenge inviting the public to attempt K4 [...] In September 2025, journalists Jarett Kobek and Richard Byrne discovered several documents among papers donated by Jim Sanborn to Smithsonian's Archives of American Art containing scraps of text that, when assembled together, produced what appeared likely to be the full plaintext of K4 [...] they submitted this text to Sanborn, who confirmed its accuracy, explaining that he had mistakenly included those scraps in the donated archives while compiling documents during cancer treatment years earlier. Shortly thereafter, Sanborn asked the Smithsonian to seal the relevant files for the next 50 years (until 2075), and they complied. [...] running from 16 October to 20 November 2025

gancho: Usada direito, a cifra de chave única é inquebrável. Pressionados pela guerra, os soviéticos fizeram cerca de 35 mil páginas de chave repetidas, e por essa brecha os EUA acharam espiões no projeto da bomba atômica.
explicacao: No sistema soviético, palavras e letras primeiro viravam números por meio de um livro de código, e depois se somava a eles uma chave tirada de blocos de uso único. Usado corretamente, esse método não pode ser quebrado. Só que produzir os blocos era lento e trabalhoso, e a guerra com a Alemanha, a partir de junho de 1941, fez disparar a demanda por mensagens cifradas. Sob a pressão do avanço alemão sobre Moscou, o fabricante soviético produziu cerca de 35 mil páginas com números de chave duplicados, todas em 1942. Para reduzir o risco, as cópias foram enviadas a usuários distantes entre si, mas analistas americanos do projeto Venona, iniciado em 1943, perceberam a repetição. Richard Hallock notou primeiro o reuso, em mensagens sobre comércio, e Meredith Gardner partiu desse material para reconstruir o livro de código. Em 20 de dezembro de 1946, Gardner fez a primeira quebra, que revelou espionagem soviética no Projeto Manhattan; entre os nomes identificados depois estão Klaus Fuchs e Julius Rosenberg. Só uma pequena parte do tráfego pôde ser lida. As páginas repetidas foram usadas quase todas até o fim de 1945, algumas até 1948, e depois disso as mensagens soviéticas voltaram a ser totalmente ilegíveis.

fontes.trecho: The VENONA Project was initiated on February 1, 1943 [...] When used correctly, the one-time pad encryption system, which has been used for all the most-secret military and diplomatic communication since the 1930s, is unbreakable. However, due to a serious blunder on the part of the Soviets, some of this traffic was vulnerable to cryptanalysis. The Soviet company that manufactured the one-time pads produced around 35,000 pages of duplicate key numbers, as a result of pressures brought about by the German advance on Moscow during World War II. The duplication—which undermines the security of a one-time system—was discovered, and attempts to lessen its impact were made by sending the duplicates to widely separated users. Despite this, the reuse was detected by cryptanalysts in the US. [...] The Soviet systems in general used a code to convert words and letters into numbers, to which additive keys (from one-time pads) were added, encrypting the content. When used correctly  one-time pad encryption is unbreakable. [...] However, cryptanalysis by American code-breakers revealed that some of the one-time pad material had incorrectly been reused by the Soviets (specifically, entire pages, although not complete books), which allowed decryption of a small part of the traffic. Generating the one-time pads was a slow and labor-intensive process, and the outbreak of war with Germany in June 1941 caused a sudden increase in the need for coded messages. [...] It was Arlington Hall's Lieutenant Richard Hallock, working on Soviet "Trade" traffic (so called because these messages dealt with Soviet trade issues), who first discovered that the Soviets were reusing pages. [...] A young Meredith Gardner then used this material to break into what turned out to be NKVD (and later GRU) traffic by reconstructing the code used to convert text to numbers. [...] On December 20, 1946, Gardner made the first break into the code, revealing the existence of Soviet espionage in the Manhattan Project. [...] All the duplicate one-time pad pages were produced in 1942, and almost all of them had been used by the end of 1945, with a few being used as late as 1948. After this, Soviet message traffic reverted to being completely unreadable. [...] Identities soon emerged of American, Canadian, Australian, and British spies in service to the Soviet government, including Klaus Fuchs, Alan Nunn May, and Donald Maclean. [...] Among those identified are Julius and Ethel Rosenberg

gancho: A criptografia de chave pública, que protege a internet, foi concebida primeiro em segredo, na inteligência britânica. Clifford Cocks chegou ao futuro RSA em 1973 sem anotar nada na hora. Tudo ficou oculto até 1997.
explicacao: Em 1970, James Ellis, engenheiro do GCHQ, a agência britânica de comunicações, propôs num relatório interno secreto o que chamou de "cifragem não secreta". Ele contou que a ideia surgiu ao ler um trabalho da Segunda Guerra, do Bell Labs, que protegia conversas por voz fazendo o próprio receptor somar um ruído aleatório à linha e depois subtraí-lo. Faltava uma função de mão única adequada, e várias pessoas tentaram criá-la sem sucesso. Clifford Cocks, especializado em teoria dos números em Oxford, entrou na agência em setembro de 1973, ouviu falar da proposta e decidiu usar a fatoração em números primos. Desenvolveu rapidamente o que depois ficou conhecido como algoritmo RSA, sem nem escrever nada na hora. O GCHQ não encontrou um jeito de usar aquilo e o tratou como segredo. Em 1977, Rivest, Shamir e Adleman inventaram o algoritmo de forma independente e o batizaram com suas iniciais; não há indício de vazamento. Em 1987, o GCHQ pensava em revelar o trabalho, mas o livro de memórias Spycatcher, de um ex-agente do MI5, adiou a divulgação em dez anos. Em 18 de dezembro de 1997, Cocks contou a história numa palestra pública. Ellis tinha morrido em 25 de novembro, um mês antes.

fontes.trecho: In the early 1970s, while working at the United Kingdom Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), he developed an early public-key cryptography (PKC) system. This pre-dated commercial offerings, but due to the classified nature of Cocks' work, it did not become widely known until 1997 when the work was declassified. [...] He continued as a PhD student at the University of Oxford, where he specialised in number theory under Bryan Birch [...] Cocks left Oxford to join Communications-Electronics Security Group (CESG), an arm of GCHQ, in September 1973. Soon after, Nick Patterson told Cocks about James H. Ellis' non-secret encryption, an idea which had been published in 1969 but never successfully implemented. Several people had attempted creating the required one-way functions, but Cocks, with his background in number theory, decided to use prime factorization, and did not even write it down at the time. With this insight, he quickly developed what later became known as the RSA encryption algorithm. GCHQ was not able to find a way to use the algorithm, and treated it as classified information. [...] In 1977, the algorithm was independently invented and published by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, who named it after their initials. There is no evidence of a hint or leak, conscious or unconscious, and Cocks has dismissed the idea. The British achievement remained secret until 1997. [...] In 1987, the GCHQ had plans to release the work, but Peter Wright's Spycatcher MI5 memoir caused them to delay revealing the research by ten years. 24 years after its discovery, on 18 December 1997, Cocks revealed the GCHQ history of public-key research in a public talk. James Ellis had died on 25 November 1997, a month before the public announcement was made.

James Henry Ellis (25 September 1924 – 25 November 1997) was a British engineer and cryptographer. [...] Ellis first proposed his scheme for "non-secret encryption" in 1970, in a (then) secret GCHQ internal report "The Possibility of Secure Non-Secret Digital Encryption". Ellis said that the idea first occurred to him after reading a paper from World War II by someone at Bell Labs describing the scheme named Project C43, a way to protect voice communications by the receiver adding (and then later subtracting) random noise.

gancho: Em 1977, os criadores do RSA desafiaram os leitores da Scientific American com uma cifra. Um deles estimou 40 quatrilhões de anos para fatorar um número parecido. Entre 1993 e 1994, mais de 600 voluntários a quebraram.
explicacao: O desafio saiu na coluna de jogos matemáticos de Martin Gardner, na edição de agosto de 1977. Ler a mensagem exigia fatorar um número de 129 algarismos, o RSA-129: a dificuldade de quebrar o RSA está ligada à de fatorar números grandes. Ron Rivest calculou que, com o melhor algoritmo e os computadores mais rápidos da época, fatorar um número de 125 algarismos levaria 40 quatrilhões de anos. A conta subestimou o futuro: os algoritmos de fatoração eram pouco estudados e avançaram muito nas décadas seguintes. Em 1993 e 1994, um projeto coordenado pela internet, um dos primeiros desse tipo, juntou mais de 600 voluntários e cerca de 1.600 máquinas, duas delas aparelhos de fax, durante seis meses. Eles usaram o crivo quadrático, inventado por Carl Pomerance em 1981. A frase escondida era "The Magic Words are Squeamish Ossifrage". Ossifrage, "quebra-ossos" em latim, é um nome antigo do abutre-barbudo, famoso por soltar ossos sobre pedras para quebrá-los. O prêmio de US$ 100 foi doado à Free Software Foundation, e a expressão "squeamish ossifrage" virou tradição em desafios de criptoanálise. Em 2015, o mesmo número foi fatorado em cerca de um dia, com uns US$ 30 de computação em nuvem.

fontes.titulo: The Magic Words are Squeamish Ossifrage
fontes.trecho: "The Magic Words are Squeamish Ossifrage" was the solution to a challenge ciphertext posed by the inventors of the RSA cipher in 1977. The problem appeared in Martin Gardner's Mathematical Games column in the August 1977 issue of Scientific American. It was solved in 1993–94 by a large, joint computer project co-ordinated by Derek Atkins, Michael Graff, Arjen Lenstra and Paul Leyland. More than 600 volunteers contributed CPU time from about 1,600 machines (two of which were fax machines) over six months. The coordination was done via the Internet and was one of the first such projects. Ossifrage ('bone-breaker', from Latin) is an older name for the bearded vulture, a scavenger famous for dropping animal bones and live tortoises on top of rocks to crack them open. The 1993–94 effort began the tradition of using the words "squeamish ossifrage" in cryptanalytic challenges. The difficulty of breaking the RSA cipher—recovering a plaintext message given a ciphertext and the public key—is connected to the difficulty of factoring large numbers. [...] The decryption of the 1977 ciphertext involved the factoring of a 129-digit (426 bit) number, RSA-129, in order to recover the plaintext. Ron Rivest estimated in 1977 that factoring a 125-digit semiprime would require 40 quadrillion years, using the best algorithm known and the fastest computers of the day. [...] However, efficient factoring algorithms had not been studied much at the time, and a lot of progress was made in the following decades. Atkins et al. used the quadratic sieve algorithm invented by Carl Pomerance in 1981. [...] There was a US$100 prize associated with the challenge, which the winners donated to the Free Software Foundation. In 2015, the same RSA-129 number was factored in about one day, with the CADO-NFS open source implementation of the number field sieve, using a commercial cloud computing service for about $30.

gancho: Segundo Heródoto, um governante grego raspou a cabeça de um escravo de confiança, tatuou nela uma mensagem e esperou o cabelo crescer. Só então o mandou ao destino, levando escondido um chamado à revolta contra a Pérsia.
explicacao: O episódio, de 499 a.C., está entre os primeiros usos registrados de esteganografia, a arte de esconder não só o conteúdo de uma mensagem, mas a própria existência dela. Heródoto conta que Histieu, tirano de Mileto, vivia em Susa como amigo e conselheiro do rei persa Dario I e, infeliz por estar longe, quis provocar uma revolta na Jônia para voltar ao poder. Raspou a cabeça do escravo, marcou o recado no couro cabeludo e o enviou a Aristágoras, seu sobrinho e genro, com a instrução de raspar de novo a cabeça do mensageiro e ler. A mensagem mandava rebelar-se contra os persas. Aristágoras obedeceu e, com a ajuda de atenienses e erétrios, atacou e incendiou Sardes. Quando Dario soube da revolta, Histieu fingiu não saber de nada e pediu para ser mandado de volta a Mileto para combatê-la. Heródoto registra outro truque da mesma época: Demarato avisou a Grécia de um ataque escrevendo direto na madeira de uma tabuinha de escrever e só depois cobrindo-a com a camada de cera de abelha. Essas tabuinhas eram superfícies comuns e reutilizáveis para escrever.

fontes.trecho: Darius considered Histiaeus to be loyal, and asked him to come back to Susa with him as a friend and advisor. Histiaeus' nephew and son-in-law Aristagoras was left in control of Miletus. [...] However, according to Herodotus, Histiaeus was unhappy having to stay in Susa, and made plans to return to his position as King of Miletus by instigating a revolt in Ionia. In 499 BC, he shaved the head of his most trusted slave, tattooed a message on his head, and then waited for his hair to grow back. The slave was then sent to Aristagoras, who was instructed to shave the slave's head again and read the message, which told him to revolt against the Persians. Aristagoras, who was disliked by his own subjects after an expedition to Naxos ended in failure, followed Histiaeus' command, and with help from the Athenians and Eretrians, attacked and burned Sardis. When Darius learned of the revolt, he sent for Histiaeus, who pretended to have no knowledge of its origins, but asked to be sent back to Miletus to put down the revolt.

Steganography ( , STEG-ə-NOG-rə-fee) is the practice of representing information within another message or physical object, in such a manner that the presence of the concealed information would not be evident to an unsuspecting person's examination. [...] The first recorded uses of steganography can be traced back to 440 BC in Greece, when Herodotus mentions two examples in his Histories. [...] Additionally, Demaratus sent a warning about a forthcoming attack to Greece by writing it directly on the wooden backing of a wax tablet before applying its beeswax surface. Wax tablets were in common use then as reusable writing surfaces, sometimes used for shorthand.

gancho: Por volta de 1499, um abade alemão escreveu um livro que parecia ensinar a usar espíritos para mandar recados a distância. A obra entrou no índice de livros proibidos. Na verdade, era um manual de escrita secreta.
explicacao: Johannes Trithemius, abade beneditino e polímata, chamou a obra de Steganographia, do grego para "escrita coberta", e foi esse o primeiro uso registrado da palavra esteganografia. Os três volumes parecem tratar de magia, com invocações de anjos. Trithemius descreveu o livro numa carta a Arnold Bostius, que morreu antes de recebê-la; colegas leram e publicaram a carta e acusaram o abade de conversar com demônios. Outro estudioso, convidado a ler a obra, jogou-a fora dizendo que o autor era um mago, e Trithemius desistiu do livro. Ele só foi impresso em Frankfurt em 1606, junto com uma chave de leitura. Ela mostrou que os dois primeiros volumes tratavam de criptografia e esteganografia: cada "anjo" correspondia a um método de esconder mensagens, e as invocações eram só o texto de fachada. Mesmo assim, em 1609 a obra entrou no Índice dos Livros Proibidos, de onde só saiu em 1900. O terceiro volume continuou sendo visto como pura magia até o fim dos anos 1990, quando Jim Reeds e Thomas Ernst, cada um por sua conta, descobriram que ele também escondia métodos de escrita secreta.

fontes.trecho: Steganographia is a book on steganography, written in c. 1499 by the German Benedictine abbot and polymath Johannes Trithemius. [...] Trithemius' most famous work, Steganographia (written c.1499; published Frankfurt, 1606), was placed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum in 1609 and removed in 1900. This book is in three volumes, and appears to be about magic—specifically, about using spirits to communicate over long distances. However, since the publication of a decryption key to the first two volumes in 1606, they were discovered to be actually concerned with cryptography and steganography. Until 1996, the third volume was widely believed to be solely about magic, but the "magical" formulas have now been shown to be covertexts for yet more material on cryptography.

The word steganography comes from Greek steganographia, which combines the words steganós (στεγανός), meaning "covered or concealed", and -graphia (γραφή) meaning "writing". The first recorded use of the term was in 1499 by Johannes Trithemius in his Steganographia, a treatise on cryptography and steganography, disguised as a book on magic. [...] a book seemingly about summoning angels to hide messages. In reality however, the book was about steganography, the angel summoning being a cover text. Every angel corresponded to a different method of steganography. He had written a letter to Arnold Bostius about his book, how it contained many methods of secret writing [...] Bostius had died before he could receive the letter, however his colleagues had read and published it, accusing him of conversing with demons. Trithemius had also invited Charles de Bovelles to read his book before de Bovelles threw it away, claiming Trithemius was a magician. This situation led Trithemius to quit the book, not however, his interest in steganography. [...] However, Book III was still widely regarded as a work of magic, with no clear way to extract its secrets. It would take until the late 1990s when Jim Reeds and Thomas Ernst independently discovered that it too, was secretly a work of steganography.

gancho: Na Primeira Guerra, os alemães quebravam códigos americanos. Um coronel resolveu usar soldados choctaw falando a própria língua. Sem palavra para "metralhadora", eles diziam "arma pequena atira rápido".
explicacao: Os alemães falavam ótimo inglês e já tinham interceptado e quebrado códigos militares dos EUA. Na França, o coronel Alfred Bloor, do 142º Regimento de Infantaria, ouviu dois soldados choctaw conversando e não entendeu nada. Concluiu que, se ele não entendia, os alemães também não entenderiam, por melhor que fosse o inglês deles; além disso, muitas línguas indígenas americanas nunca tinham sido escritas. Com a cooperação dos soldados, montou e testou o código. O primeiro teste em combate foi em 26 de outubro de 1918, na retirada delicada de duas companhias, que deu certo. Segundo Bloor, a surpresa total do inimigo mostrava que ele não conseguia decifrar as mensagens, e um oficial alemão capturado confirmou que estavam completamente confusos com a língua. O choctaw, porém, não tinha termos para tudo, e os soldados improvisaram: "arma grande" para artilharia e "arma pequena atira rápido" para metralhadora. Cherokees e lakotas também foram pioneiros dessa prática na mesma guerra, e a ideia foi retomada em escala bem maior pelos navajos na Segunda Guerra. Os próprios choctaw, ao que parece, não se chamavam de code talkers: a expressão só surgiu durante ou depois da Segunda Guerra.

fontes.trecho: The German forces proved not only to speak excellent English but also to have intercepted and broken American military codes. An American officer, Colonel Alfred Wainwright Bloor, noticed a number of American Indians serving with him in the 142nd Infantry in France. Overhearing two Choctaw Indians speaking with each another, he realized he could not understand them. He also realized that if he could not understand them, the same would be true for Germans, no matter how good their English skills. Besides, many Native American languages have never been written down. With the active cooperation of his Choctaw soldiers, Colonel Bloor tested and deployed a code, using the Choctaw language in place of regular military code. The first combat test took place on October 26, 1918, when Colonel Bloor ordered a "delicate" withdrawal of two companies of the 2nd Battalion, from Chufilly to Chardeny. The movement was successful: "The enemy's complete surprise is evidence that he could not decipher the messages", Bloor observed. A captured German officer confirmed they were "completely confused by the Indian language and gained no benefit whatsoever" from their wiretaps. [...] He noted, however, that the Choctaw tongue, by itself, was unable to fully express the military terminology then in use. No Choctaw word or phrase existed to describe a "machine gun", for example. So the Choctaws improvised, using their words for "big gun" to describe "artillery" and "little gun shoot fast" for "machine gun." [...] Later, other tribes would use their languages for the military in various units, most notably the Navajo in World War II. [...] The Choctaw themselves appear not to have referred to themselves as 'code talkers'. The phrase was not coined until during or after World War II.
Early pioneers of Native American-based communications used by the US military included the Cherokee, Choctaw, and Lakota peoples during World War I.

gancho: Um manuscrito cifrado do século XVIII, com 75 mil caracteres, foi decifrado em 2011 com ajuda de computador. Revelou os ritos de uma sociedade secreta alemã: num deles, o candidato tinha um fio da sobrancelha arrancado.
explicacao: O Copiale tem 105 páginas encadernadas e ficou indecifrado por mais de 260 anos. As únicas palavras legíveis eram "Copiales 3", no fim, e "Philipp 1866", na folha de guarda. Kevin Knight, da Universidade do Sul da Califórnia, especialista em tradução automática, e Beáta Megyesi e Christiane Schaefer, da Universidade de Uppsala, encararam a cifra como se fosse uma língua estrangeira. A comparação com 80 línguas indicou que o original era provavelmente alemão, como o nome "Philipp", na grafia alemã, já sugeria. Havia um truque: as letras latinas sem acento, que pareciam ser o texto, só marcavam espaços. As letras de verdade vinham codificadas em letras acentuadas, gregas e símbolos, e sete caracteres diferentes valiam o mesmo "e". Megyesi notou que um símbolo significava "olho", e Schaefer ligou isso aos Oculistas, sociedade secreta de Wolfenbüttel que usava a visão como metáfora do conhecimento. O manuscrito é dos anos 1730. As 16 primeiras páginas descrevem a iniciação: o candidato devia ler um papel em branco, recebia óculos, tentava de novo, lavava os olhos com um pano e, por fim, passava por uma "operação" em que lhe arrancavam um único fio da sobrancelha. O próprio manuscrito sugere que os Oculistas, ou ao menos o conde Veltheim, que os liderava, eram maçons preservando ritos proibidos pouco antes pelo papa Clemente XII.

fontes.trecho: The Copiale cipher is an encrypted manuscript created in the 1700s and consisting of 75,000 handwritten characters filling 105 pages in a bound volume. Undeciphered for more than 260 years, the document was decrypted in 2011 with computer assistance. An international team consisting of Kevin Knight of the University of Southern California Information Sciences Institute and Viterbi School of Engineering, along with Beáta Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer of Uppsala University in Sweden, found the cipher to be an encrypted German text. [...] Decipherment revealed that the document had been created in the 1730s by a secret society called the "high enlightened (Hocherleuchtete) oculist order" of Wolfenbüttel, or Oculists. The Oculists used sight as a metaphor for knowledge. [...] The only plain text in the book is "Copiales 3" at the end and "Philipp 1866" on the flyleaf. [...] The plain text letters of the message were found to be encoded by accented Roman letters, Greek letters and symbols, with unaccented Roman letters serving only to represent spaces. The researchers found that the initial 16 pages describe an Oculist initiation ceremony. The manuscript portrays, among other things, an initiation ritual in which the candidate is asked to read a blank piece of paper and, on confessing inability to do so, is given eyeglasses and asked to try again, and then again after washing the eyes with a cloth, followed by an "operation" in which a single eyebrow hair is plucked. [...] Seven ciphertext characters encode the single letter "e". [...] A machine translation expert, Knight approached language translation as if all languages were ciphers [...] A comparison with 80 languages confirmed that the original language was likely German, which the researchers had guessed based on the word "Philipp," a German spelling. [...] Megyesi later realized that a particular symbol meant "eye", and Schaefer connected that discovery to the Oculists. [...] The Philipp 1866 Copiales 3 document, however, appears to suggest that the Oculists, or at least Count Veltheim, were a group of Freemasons who created the Oculist society in order to pass along the Masonic rites which had recently been banned by Pope Clement XII. [...] The Oculists were a group of ophthalmologists led by Count Friedrich August von Veltheim

gancho: Um panfleto americano do século XIX prometia um tesouro enterrado, descrito em três textos cifrados. Um foi lido usando a Declaração de Independência como chave. Aplicada a outro, a mesma chave dá "abcdefghiijklmmnohpp".
explicacao: Segundo o panfleto The Beale Papers, um certo Thomas J. Beale enterrou ouro, prata e joias no condado de Bedford, na Virgínia, e deixou com o dono de uma hospedaria três mensagens cifradas: o local, a descrição do tesouro e os nomes dos donos. A segunda foi resolvida como uma cifra de livro: cada número indica uma palavra da Declaração de Independência dos EUA, e vale a primeira letra dela. O 115, por exemplo, aponta para "instituted", que dá a letra I. A chave só funciona com uma versão ligeiramente diferente da Declaração e com erros de numeração corrigidos. O texto decifrado descreve o tesouro guardado em potes de barro com tampas de ferro. Os outros dois textos nunca foram lidos, e todas as buscas fracassaram. Quando a mesma Declaração é usada no primeiro texto, surgem sequências alfabéticas como "abcdefghiijklmmnohpp"; segundo a American Cryptogram Association, a chance de isso se repetir por acaso é menor que uma em cem trilhões. Há muitos argumentos de que tudo é uma farsa. O pesquisador Joe Nickell apontou palavras anacrônicas para a época, como "stampeding", e, pelo estilo, concluiu que "Beale" era quase certamente James B. Ward, que publicou o panfleto. Outros acham que os dois textos ainda escondem uma mensagem.

fontes.trecho: The Beale ciphers are a set of three ciphertexts, one of which allegedly states the location of a buried treasure of gold, silver and jewels [...] Comprising three ciphertexts, the first (unsolved) text describes the location, the second (solved) ciphertext accounts the content of the treasure, and the third (unsolved) lists the names of the treasure's owners and their next of kin. The story of the three ciphertexts originates from an 1867 pamphlet called The Beale Papers, detailing treasure being buried by a man named Thomas J. Beale in a secret location in Bedford County, Virginia, in about 1820. Beale entrusted a box containing the encrypted messages to a local innkeeper named Robert Morriss and then disappeared, never to be seen again. [...] Since the publication of the pamphlet, a number of attempts have been made to decode the two remaining ciphertexts and to locate the treasure, but all efforts have resulted in failure. There are many arguments that the entire story is a hoax, including the 1980 article "A Dissenting Opinion" by cryptographer Jim Gillogly, and a 1982 scholarly analysis of The Beale Papers and their related story by Joe Nickell, using historical records that cast doubt on the existence of Thomas J. Beale. Nickell also presented linguistic evidence demonstrating anachronisms—words such as "stampeding", for instance, are of later vintage. His analysis of the writing style showed that Beale was almost certainly James B. Ward, whose 1885 pamphlet brought the Beale ciphers to light. [...] The friend, then using an edition of the United States Declaration of Independence as the key for a modified book cipher, successfully deciphered the second ciphertext which gave a description of the buried treasure. [...] The above is securely packed in clay pots, with iron covers. [...] To decrypt it, one finds the word corresponding to the number (e.g., the first number is 115, and the 115th word in the Declaration of Independence is "instituted"), and takes the first letter of that word (in the case of the example, "I"). Beale used a version of the United States Declaration of Independence slightly different from the original, and made mistakes in numbering it. [...] the two undeciphered ones did not show the patterns one would expect of randomly chosen numbers and probably encoded an intelligible text. [...] If the modified Declaration of Independence is used as a key for the first cipher, it yields alphabetical sequences such as abcdefghiijklmmnohpp and others. According to the American Cryptogram Association, the chances of such sequences appearing multiple times in the one ciphertext by chance are less than one in a hundred million million.
